hints: Focus on the special language here, initiation, propagation and termination are only ever used for one type of mechanism.
Look for an alkane reacting with a halogen in UV light, as that is the classic example that uses free radicals.
Check which equation swaps a hydrogen for a chlorine to make an alkyl chloride plus HCl, and you will have the match.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the mechanism fingerprint**

Those three words are the fingerprint for free radical substitution. No other A Level mechanism uses them. Initiation makes radicals, propagation keeps them going, termination removes them.

**Recall the classic example**

The classic free radical substitution is an alkane with a halogen, usually chlorine or bromine in UV light:
$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$
Initiation is homolytic fission: $$\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^\bullet$$

**Match to the options**

Only option A shows an alkane, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$, reacting with $\text{Cl}_2$ to give substitution products. The others are nucleophilic substitution, electrophilic addition and nucleophilic addition, none of which involve radicals.

options.A: Correct. This is free radical substitution of butane by chlorine. It proceeds by initiation to form Cl radicals, propagation steps where Cl radical abstracts H and alkyl radical reacts with Cl2, and termination where two radicals combine.
options.B: Incorrect. This is nucleophilic substitution of a bromoalkane by OH- to form an alcohol. It proceeds by SN1 or SN2 with a nucleophile, not by radicals, so there are no initiation, propagation or termination steps.
options.C: Incorrect. This is electrophilic addition of water to an alkene to form an alcohol. It proceeds via a carbocation intermediate attacked by water, not via free radicals.
options.D: Incorrect. This is nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde to form a hydroxynitrile (cyanohydrin). It proceeds by attack of CN- nucleophile on the carbonyl carbon, with no radicals involved.
